subagent_reports.topic: Destructive triage command architecture validation — fusing report + executable destruction into /adv-cleanup under one shared approval tier

sources.label: clig.dev — Command Line Interface Guidelines (Confirm before doing anything dangerous; -n/--dry-run; -f/--force)
sources.summary: Canonical CLI design guidance. Tiered danger model: Mild (delete a file, maybe prompt), Moderate (delete a directory / remote resource / bulk mod that can't be easily undone — prompt + offer dry-run), Severe (delete entire app/server — make hard to confirm by accident, type name-of-thing, --confirm flag). Explicitly flags implicit bulk deletion (config 10->1 deletes 9 things) as severe risk that must be hard to do by accident. Endorses y/yes + -f/--force convention; -n/--dry-run is a standard flag.

sources.label: The CLI Spec (clispec.dev) — Principles 4 & 5
sources.summary: 'Reserve new confirmation gates for genuinely destructive or irreversible operations, and introduce them as deliberate design decisions.' Non-TTY must refuse with confirmation_required error naming bypass flag, never proceed silently. Endorses --dry-run with structured output for destructive ops.

sources.label: peterc — A compact contract for CLIs for agents and dev tools (2026-06-06 gist)
sources.summary: Sharpest direct guidance on risk asymmetry: 'Classify danger by decision tests... More danger tests matched => stronger guard. Low-risk reversible local changes may skip confirmation; bulk/remote/irreversible changes get confirmation plus --dry-run; high-impact named targets require typed target or --confirm=<name>.' Dry-run plan schema includes per-resource reversible:false field and per-plan risks:['remote_state','irreversible'].

sources.label: Docker — docker system prune reference
sources.summary: FUSED report+execute. Single command discovers AND deletes unused containers/networks/images/cache. Defaults to interactive [y/N]; -f/--force skips. --volumes escalates scope. No separate plan command.

sources.label: Kubernetes — kubectl delete --dry-run=none|client|server
sources.summary: FUSED. --dry-run tri-state: none (real delete), client (print only), server (validate admission, do not persist). --force 'may result in inconsistency or data loss and requires confirmation'.

sources.label: Git — git-prune(1)
sources.summary: FUSED. -n/--dry-run reports what it would remove. git gc wraps git prune. Both are single-command discover+destroy.

sources.label: Git — git-branch(1) (-d vs -D)
sources.summary: -d/--delete: branch must be fully merged in upstream/HEAD; refuses unmerged. 'If the branch currently has a reflog then the reflog will also be deleted.' -D = --delete --force. --merged/--no-merged filters for safe-delete candidates.

sources.label: Git — git-reflog(1) (recoverability window)
sources.summary: HEAD reflog records all branch updates. gc.reflogExpire defaults 90d (reachable), gc.reflogExpireUnreachable 30d. Branch deleted via -d recoverable via HEAD reflog SHA lookup for ~30-90d before gc prunes. Time-bounded recovery.

sources.label: Git — git-worktree (remove safety)
sources.summary: git worktree remove refuses modified/untracked tracked files unless --force. Confirms ADV tool's 'refuses dirty/unmerged' claim is consistent with git defaults. Worktree removal deletes working dir but branch + commits remain intact.

sources.label: Terraform — terraform apply / destroy
sources.summary: HYBRID. plan and apply are SEPARATE commands, BUT 'terraform apply without a saved plan automatically creates a plan, prompts, and performs operations' — fused automatic-plan is the default. Saved-plan two-step exists for CI/automation reproducibility. terraform destroy is a convenience alias for apply -destroy.

sources.label: Terraform — destroy typed confirmation
sources.summary: terraform destroy requires typing literal 'yes' (not y): 'Only yes will be accepted to confirm. There is no undo.' Confirms Severe-tier typed-confirmation convention for irreversible infra destruction.

sources.label: GitHub — Deleting a repository (typed name confirmation)
sources.summary: Multi-step + TYPED name confirmation: click Delete -> 'I want to delete' -> 'I have read and understand' -> TYPE THE REPO NAME -> Delete. 'permanently delete team permissions. cannot be undone.' 90-day restore window for some repos.

sources.label: AWS CLI — ec2 terminate-instances
sources.summary: WARNING: 'Terminating an instance is permanent and irreversible.' --dry-run checks PERMISSIONS ONLY, does not preview deletion. NO interactive CLI prompt — protection delegated to API-layer termination-protection. Demonstrates irreversible-op protection can live at a different layer than the CLI prompt.

sources.label: npm — npm prune
sources.summary: FUSED. --dry-run makes no changes. --json prints what was/would-be removed. No separate plan command; no confirmation prompt by default (Mild).

sources.label: cargo-sweep
sources.summary: FUSED. --dry-run 'recommended as a first step'. --recursive for bulk. No confirmation prompt (build-artifact deletion = Mild/recoverable by rebuild).

sources.label: nix-collect-garbage (source)
sources.summary: FUSED. --dry-run prints what would be freed; without it, deletes. --delete-old/-d escalates to remove old profile generations (comment: 'makes rollbacks to before this point impossible'). Explicit acknowledgment that -d crosses into irreversible territory.

sources.label: Arcjet — Designing a CLI for AI agents (confirmation envelope)
sources.summary: Non-interactive confirmation protocol: mutation without --confirm returns exit 4 + JSON envelope. 'No fuzzy suggestions means a typo stays a typo. Structured confirmations mean a human cannot just hammer through a prompt.' Validates whitelist-only (no fuzzy) prompt design.

sources.label: anc.dev/p5 — CLI principles for agents
sources.summary: Every write op MUST support --dry-run. 'Destructive operations require explicit --force or --yes. Without it, the tool refuses or enters dry-run. It MUST NOT mutate silently.' Read-vs-write distinction must be visible from name and --help.

subagent_reports.architecture_assessment: The FUSED report+execute pattern is well-established and correct for a hygiene/prune command (docker system prune, git prune/gc, kubectl delete --dry-run, npm prune, cargo sweep, nix-collect-garbage all fuse; even terraform's separated plan/apply has a fused automatic-plan default). ADV /adv-cleanup fits this category and should NOT be split into separate commands. The dry-run-default + whitelist-only-regex approval design is also canonical (clig.dev endorses y/yes + -f; clig.dev/Arcjet explicitly endorse NO fuzzy matching). HOWEVER, putting REVERSIBLE (ADV change close, metadata) and IRREVERSIBLE (worktree dir delete, branch -d) operations behind the SAME --execute flag and SAME 'approve all' prompt is in tension with three independent authoritative sources: clig.dev's Severe-tier guidance (line 820-826), clispec.dev Principle 4 ('reserve confirmation gates for genuinely destructive or irreversible operations'), and peterc's compact contract ('More danger tests matched => stronger guard... irreversible changes get confirmation plus --dry-run'). The recoverability analysis partially mitigates severity (worktree delete is actually LOW risk because branch+commits survive; branch -d is MODERATE because time-bounded reflog recovery ~30-90d; only the directory removal and ref+reflog are truly gone), but it does NOT collapse the asymmetry: change-close is zero-effort reversible, while branch -d requires reflog archaeology under a time deadline. One shared tier is therefore defensible only if each irreversible bucket receives a distinct, name-listing sub-prompt; a single bulk 'approve all' covering reversible+irreversible together is the clig.dev line-826 'easy to do by accident' anti-pattern.

validation.notes: Pattern (fused report+execute) = Confirmed. Approval-mechanism shape (whitelist regex, no fuzzy) = Confirmed adequate. Risk-tiering (single shared tier for reversible + irreversible) = Caution. No hard blocker because (a) recoverability is real and reduces blast radius, (b) no single canonical source names the exact 'do not combine tiers' anti-pattern, (c) underlying git tools already enforce their own safety refusals. But three independent authoritative CLI-design sources converge on 'stronger guard for irreversible' and the design as described does not implement that stronger guard for the destructive buckets.

tradeoffs: Fused command = better UX/discoverability (one command, --execute escalates), matches docker/git/kubectl norm; cost = one flag controls mixed-severity actions.
Whitelist-only regex prompt = deterministic, scriptable, typo-safe (Arcjet/clig.dev endorse); cost = no fuzzy forgiveness, which is correct not a deficiency.

Shared tier for reversible+irreversible = simpler implementation, one code path; cost = a user who routinely types 'approve all' for harmless hygiene closure can accidentally destroy worktrees/branches — the precise clig.dev line-826 'implicit bulk deletion' footgun.

Recoverability reduces blast radius (worktree dir trivially recreatable; branch -d recoverable via HEAD reflog ~30-90d); cost = recovery is not zero-effort and is time-bounded, so it cannot be classified as the same tier as metadata-only change-close.

alternatives_considered.option: Fully fused single-tier (proposed design as described)
alternatives_considered.rationale: Fused command pattern is correct; single shared approval tier for reversible+irreversible is in tension with clig.dev Severe-tier, clispec.dev P4, and peterc compact-contract guidance. Modify, do not reject.

No canonical precedent for prune/hygiene tools. docker system prune, git prune/gc, kubectl delete, npm prune, cargo sweep, nix-collect-garbage ALL fuse. terraform's plan/apply split exists for infra-provisioning reproducibility in CI, not because fused is unsafe. Splitting violates the established pattern and adds UX friction without safety benefit.

alternatives_considered.option: Fused command + tiered confirmation (separate escalation flag/prompt for irreversible buckets)
alternatives_considered.rationale: Preserves the established fused pattern. Adds a second escalation gate (e.g. --execute-destructive, or --execute --include=worktrees,branches) AND a per-bucket name-listing prompt for each irreversible bucket. Matches clig.dev Severe-tier 'make it hard to confirm by accident' + peterc per-resource reversible:false field. Two-stage escalation is the minimal change that resolves the asymmetry.

alternatives_considered.option: Typed confirmation (type resource name/count) for ALL buckets including reversible change-close
alternatives_considered.rationale: Overkill for reversible metadata change-close (clig.dev Mild tier: 'you might want to prompt, you might not'). Typed confirmation reserved for Severe/irreversible/named-target ops. Universal application adds friction without proportional safety gain.

architecture_judgement.recommendation: VERDICT: Caution. Proceed with fused report+execute in /adv-cleanup (Confirmed pattern). BUT add a distinct second-tier confirmation for the two irreversible buckets (worktree delete + branch delete). Concrete shape: (1) keep --execute enabling only reversible change-closure; (2) introduce a separate escalation flag (e.g. --execute-destructive, or --execute --include=worktrees,branches) that must ALSO be set for irreversible buckets to be eligible; (3) each irreversible bucket gets its OWN per-bucket prompt listing exact resource names/paths being destroyed (not a bulk 'approve all' that mixes reversible+irreversible); (4) surface per-bucket reversible:false in the dry-run report (matches peterc compact-contract dry-run schema). Keep the whitelist-only regex parser; do NOT add fuzzy matching (Arcjet/clig.dev: typos should stay typos). Do NOT split into separate commands.

subagent_reports.recommendation: See architecture_judgement.recommendation. Summary: Caution verdict. Fused command = keep. Shared single-tier approval for reversible+irreversible = adjust to two-stage escalation + per-bucket name-listing prompts for irreversible buckets. Whitelist regex parser = keep as-is (no fuzzy).
follow_ups: Could not read the actual current /adv-cleanup implementation to confirm the exact approval-prompt shape and whether 'approve all' today truly spans all buckets in one prompt or is already per-bucket — relied on task description. Verify against plugin/src/tools or the command packet before implementing the tier split.

Could not find a single canonical source that explicitly names 'combining reversible and irreversible behind one confirmation flag' as a named anti-pattern; the guidance is convergent-but-implicit across clig.dev (tiered danger), clispec.dev (reserve gates for destructive/irreversible), and peterc compact-contract (per-resource reversible field + stronger guard for irreversible). Verdict rests on convergence of three sources, not a single normative citation.

Did not verify the ADV underlying worktree-deletion tool's specific safety refusals beyond confirming git worktree remove's default refuses dirty trees without --force. If the ADV tool goes beyond git's defaults (e.g. refuses unpushed branches, process-CWD worktrees), document those as defense-in-depth in the bucket prompt so the user sees the safety net.

Branch -d recoverability window (~30-90d via HEAD reflog before gc.reflogExpireUnreachable prunes) should be surfaced in the destructive-bucket prompt so the user understands recovery is time-bounded, not indefinite.

documents.proposal:
## Intent

`/adv-cleanup` today triages only one hygiene surface — active ADV changes — and buckets them as duplicate, stuck-at-proposal, abandoned-mid-flight, or ready-to-archive. It also emits a single report-only worktree drift line sourced from `adv_worktree_triage`, then explicitly disowns deletion: "`/adv-cleanup` never deletes worktrees."

Two further hygiene surfaces are entirely invisible to the command:

1. **Archived-branch debt** — local `change/*` branches tied to archived ADV changes that are fully merged and safe to delete. Discovery and deletion live in `adv_worktree_cleanup mode: "archived_branches"`, which `/adv-cleanup` never calls.
2. **Archived/closed state leaks** — leak detection and recommendations exposed by `adv_status view: "hygiene"`, which `/adv-cleanup` never calls.

The result is that a user who runs the cleanup command believes they have seen their cleanup debt, but has seen roughly half of it, and cannot act on any of the worktree/branch half without hand-running separate tools.

This change extends `/adv-cleanup` into a complete hygiene triage surface: it discovers and reports all four surfaces, and it gains executable closure buckets for safe worktree deletion and merged archived-branch deletion under the same per-bucket Tier B approval protocol that already governs change closure.

## Root Cause Analysis

Not applicable — non-defect origin. `/adv-cleanup` behaves exactly as its command contract and skill specify. The gap is incomplete scope coverage in the specification itself, not a divergence between specified and actual behavior.

## Chosen direction

User selected the widest of three offered shapes: **report + executable worktrees and branches**.

Rejected alternatives:

- *Report-only discovery* — would surface the debt but still force the user into `adv_worktree_cleanup` and `adv_status view: "hygiene"` by hand, preserving the exact split-surface problem this change exists to remove.
- *Report + executable branch bucket only* — deletes merged branches but leaves worktree deletion split off, an inconsistent boundary that is harder to explain than either extreme.

The current "never deletes worktrees" invariant is intentionally removed. Its safety value is replaced, not discarded: destructive worktree and branch actions are gated by the existing per-bucket Tier B whitelist-only approval parser, default dry-run mode, and the underlying tools' own safety refusals (`adv_worktree_delete` checks uncommitted work and integration requirements; `adv_worktree_cleanup` skips process-CWD worktrees, preserves dirty/unmerged worktrees, and only deletes fully-merged squash-safe branches).

## LBP Targets

- **Destructive-action boundary** — validate that promoting worktree/branch deletion into approval-gated closure buckets is consistent with the existing Tier B cancellation-approval contract (`rq-inlineApproval01.4`) rather than requiring a distinct approval tier.
- **Tool routing** — confirm `adv_worktree_cleanup mode: "archived_branches" dryRun: true` is the correct discovery call for merged-branch debt, and `adv_status view: "hygiene"` for archived/closed leak detection.
- **Bucket precedence interaction** — the existing precedence table is most-specific-wins over changes. New worktree/branch/leak buckets operate on different entity kinds and must not silently reorder or shadow change classification.
- **Atomicity and failure isolation** — existing rule is "each bucket is atomic; continue to next bucket after one bucket failure." Confirm this holds for partially-successful multi-worktree deletion.

## Scope

- `.opencode/command/adv-cleanup.md` — new discovery calls, report sections, approval prompts, apply rules; remove the never-deletes-worktrees disclaimer
- `skills/adv-cleanup/SKILL.md` — mirror the methodology (skill stays read-only guidance; command owns tool calls and mutation)
- `.adv/specs/` — spec-law delta for the cleanup capability, kind determined in discovery
- Command/skill asset symmetry and manifest tests
- Deployed copies refreshed via `scripts/deploy-local.sh`

Explicitly out of scope: changing `adv_worktree_delete`, `adv_worktree_cleanup`, `adv_worktree_triage`, or `adv_status` tool behavior. This change is a consumer-side orchestration extension only.

## User Outcomes

- Running `/adv-cleanup` once surfaces every hygiene surface — stale changes, drifted worktrees, merged archived branches, and archived/closed state leaks — in a single report.
- The user can act on worktree and branch debt from inside the same command, under explicit per-bucket approval, instead of hand-running separate tools.
- Dry-run remains the default; nothing destructive happens without an exact whitelist approval reply.
- Existing change-closure behavior, bucket precedence, child-lineage guard, and hot-band exclusion are unchanged.

## Spec-law impact: Add

Assessment performed against `.adv/specs/` (23 capabilities). No existing requirement governs `/adv-cleanup` triage scope — `rg -n "adv-cleanup" .adv/specs/` returns nothing. The command's behavior is defined entirely in `.opencode/command/adv-cleanup.md` and `skills/adv-cleanup/SKILL.md` with no durable spec law behind it.

Adjacent law reviewed and found compatible (no modification required):

| Requirement | Capability | Relevance | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| `rq-terminalCleanupSafety01` | worktree-lifecycle | "advWorktreeDelete is the sole deletion authority"; `census.cleanupEligible` is "advisory discovery/visibility data only and must not be used as sufficient deletion authority" | **Compatible** — cleanup must delegate deletion and must NOT treat the `adv_worktree_triage` safe bucket as authority. This constraint is load-bearing on the design. |
| `rq-terminalCleanupReaper01` | worktree-lifecycle | Reaper "must be reachable from archive, manual cleanup, status/triage discovery" | **Compatible** — `/adv-cleanup` is a manual-cleanup reach path. |
| `rq-archiveBranchCleanup01` | advance-workflow | `archived_branches` mode is "operator-explicit (no background sweeps, no daemons, no session-start auto-cleanup per P37)" | **Compatible** — user-invoked `/adv-cleanup --execute` under Tier B approval is operator-explicit. |
| `rq-inlineApproval01` | advance-workflow | Enumerates Tier A/B across the seven named gate checkpoints; `.4` defines the structured numbered-list cancellation format | **Compatible, extended not modified** — cleanup's destructive-bucket approval is a new action class outside the seven gate checkpoints. It reuses the `.4` structural pattern rather than amending it. |

### Delta obligation

Add `rq-cleanupHygieneScope01` to `.adv/specs/advance-workflow/spec.json`, priority `must`, tags `[cleanup, hygiene, approval, safety]`.

**Body.** `/adv-cleanup` MUST triage all four ADV hygiene surfaces in a single run: active-change debt, worktree drift, merged archived `change/*` branch debt, and archived/closed state leaks. Discovery MUST route through `adv_change_list`, `adv_worktree_triage`, `adv_worktree_cleanup mode: "archived_branches" dryRun: true`, and `adv_status view: "hygiene"` respectively. Dry-run remains the default mode. Buckets MUST be classified by reversibility, and irreversible buckets MUST require a stronger confirmation than reversible ones. Deletion MUST delegate to `adv_worktree_delete` / `adv_worktree_cleanup` per `rq-terminalCleanupSafety01`; `adv_worktree_triage` classification is advisory discovery data and is never deletion authority.

**Scenarios.**

- `rq-cleanupHygieneScope01.1` — Four-surface discovery.
  *Given* a project with stale changes, drifted worktrees, merged archived branches, and archived/closed state leaks; *when* the user runs `/adv-cleanup` in default dry-run mode; *then* the report contains a section for each of the four surfaces, each section is labelled with its reversibility, and no mutation occurs.

- `rq-cleanupHygieneScope01.2` — Reversibility labelling.
  *Given* a cleanup report with both reversible and irreversible candidate buckets; *when* the report is rendered; *then* every bucket carries an explicit reversible/irreversible marker, and irreversible buckets state their recovery path and any recovery time bound.

- `rq-cleanupHygieneScope01.3` — Typed confirmation for irreversible buckets.
  *Given* an irreversible bucket (worktree deletion or branch deletion) presented for approval; *when* the user replies `approve all`; *then* the reply is rejected and re-prompted, because irreversible buckets require a count-matched typed confirmation rather than the reversible-bucket whitelist.

- `rq-cleanupHygieneScope01.4` — Delegated deletion authority.
  *Given* an approved irreversible bucket; *when* the command applies it; *then* deletion is performed by `adv_worktree_delete` or `adv_worktree_cleanup`, the tools' own safety refusals are honoured and surfaced, and `adv_worktree_triage` classification alone never authorises removal.

- `rq-cleanupHygieneScope01.5` — Dry-run default preserved.
  *Given* no explicit execute flag; *when* `/adv-cleanup` runs; *then* no change is closed, no worktree is deleted, no branch is deleted, and the footer states how to re-run with execution enabled.

## LBP validation: Caution — adopted with adjustments

Independent validator (`adv-researcher`) returned **⚠️ Caution** on the "fuse report + executable destruction under one shared approval tier" decision.

**Confirmed without change.** The fused report+execute command shape is the established norm, not a deviation. Evidence surveyed: `docker system prune`, `git gc`/`git prune`, `kubectl delete --dry-run=none|client|server`, `npm prune`, `cargo sweep`, `nix-collect-garbage` all fuse discovery and destruction behind a dry-run/force flag. Even `terraform`, the canonical "separated plan/apply" example, fuses by default — `terraform apply` without a saved plan file creates a plan, prompts, and applies in one command; the two-step form exists for CI reproducibility, not safety. Splitting `/adv-cleanup` into separate discover and destroy commands was therefore rejected.

**Confirmed without change.** Dry-run default plus whitelist-only regex parsing with no fuzzy matching matches clig.dev's robustness guidance and is explicitly endorsed for agent-facing CLIs — a typo should stay a typo rather than be helpfully resolved into a destructive action. The existing parser is kept as-is for reversible buckets.

**Caution — adjustment adopted.** clig.dev's tiered danger model classifies "deleting a directory" and "complex bulk modification that can't be easily undone" as Moderate-to-Severe, and states that severe actions should be made "hard to confirm by accident", suggesting the user be asked "to type something non-trivial". clispec.dev and peterc's compact-contract independently reach the same conclusion: stronger guard for irreversible. The validator found no single normative source naming "reversible and irreversible behind one flag" as an anti-pattern, which is why the verdict is Caution rather than Conflict — but three independent sources converge on the direction.

Recoverability analysis reduces severity without collapsing the asymmetry:

| Action | Destroyed | Survives | Recovery | Tier |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ADV change close | metadata flag | full history | re-open | reversible, zero effort |
| `git branch -d` | branch ref + its reflog | commits (reachable from merge target; `-d` refuses unmerged) | `git reflog` → `git branch <name> <sha>` | irreversible, time-bounded 30–90d (`gc.reflogExpireUnreachable`=30d, `gc.reflogExpire`=90d) |
| worktree dir delete | working directory | branch + commits (tool refuses dirty/unmerged) | `git worktree add <path> <branch>` | irreversible in effect, cheap to recreate |

**Resolution.** Three shapes were offered to the user: separate `--execute-destructive` escalation flag; single flag with reversibility markers; single flag with typed confirmation at the prompt. The user selected typed confirmation, conditional on it being simple to implement. It is — these are markdown contracts, so the change is one additional reply-parsing row plus a rejection rule, the same edit cost as the weaker option.

## Design

### Surface model

Four surfaces, two reversibility classes:

| # | Surface | Discovery | Class | Executable |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Active-change debt (duplicate / stuck / abandoned / ready-to-archive) | `adv_change_list` + `adv_change_show` | reversible | yes — existing behavior, unchanged |
| 2 | Worktree drift | `adv_worktree_triage` | **irreversible** | yes — new |
| 3 | Merged archived `change/*` branches | `adv_worktree_cleanup mode: "archived_branches" dryRun: true` | **irreversible** | yes — new |
| 4 | Archived/closed state leaks | `adv_status view: "hygiene"` | report-only | no — recommendations only |

Surface 4 stays report-only because its remediation is heterogeneous (leaks route to `adv_archive_purge`, an operator-only `recoveryOnly` tool with its own approval contract) and folding that into cleanup would duplicate an existing approval surface.

### Bucket precedence is unaffected

The existing most-specific-wins precedence table orders *changes* only. New buckets operate on different entity kinds — worktrees, branches, leak records — and are classified independently. A change and its worktree may both appear, in different sections; that is correct and intended, and the report states the relationship rather than suppressing either.

### Approval model

Reversible buckets keep the current parser verbatim: `approve all` / `reject all` / `keep N,M` / `cancel N,M` / `stop`.

Irreversible buckets get a distinct prompt that:

1. Lists every candidate by number with its **exact worktree path or branch name** — never a count-only summary.
2. States the reversibility marker and the recovery path, including the reflog time bound for branch deletion.
3. **Rejects bare `approve all`.** Accepted replies are `delete all N` where `N` must equal the exact listed candidate count, `delete N,M` for a subset, `skip` to skip the bucket, and `stop`/`abort` to halt the run.
4. Re-prompts on anything else, including a count mismatch. No LLM fallback, consistent with Tier B.

The count-match requirement is the terraform-`yes` property: the confirmation cannot be produced from muscle memory, because the user must read the report to type it.

### Delegation and safety

`adv_worktree_triage` output classifies candidates for *display and selection only*. Every approved deletion is executed by `adv_worktree_delete` or `adv_worktree_cleanup`, which re-verify independently (terminal owning-change status, branch integration, clean worktree state, no live process CWD, tree-SHA squash-merge-safe branch detection). Tool refusals are surfaced verbatim in the result lines rather than retried or worked around. This satisfies `rq-terminalCleanupSafety01`'s sole-deletion-authority constraint.

Per-bucket atomicity and continue-after-bucket-failure carry over from the existing apply rules.

### Files and guards

`.opencode/command/adv-cleanup.md` (140 lines) — Phase 1 gains two discovery calls; Phase 2.5 expands from the worktree-only drift report into the four-surface hygiene report; Phase 3 gains report sections; Phase 4 gains the irreversible-bucket prompt; Phase 5 gains delegated-deletion apply rules; Key Tools gains the new tool names. The `skill("adv-cleanup")` reference and its inline fallback at L17–19 must survive — `skill-loading-policy-assets.test.ts:231–245` requires a fallback phrase in a bounded window around the reference. Spec-citation prose for `rq-inlineApproval01.3`, `rq-inlineApproval01.4`, and `rq-autonomy01` at L9 and L90 must survive or be re-cited.

`skills/adv-cleanup/SKILL.md` (191 lines) — mirrors the three sections that are verbatim duplicates of the command (Worktree Drift Report, Approval Parser, Apply Rules) plus its own Defaults, Report Shape template, Anti-Patterns, and Constraints. The skill stays read-only guidance; the command retains ownership of tool calls and mutation.

`plugin/src/adv-cleanup-contract-assets.test.ts` (63 lines) — the only behavioral guard on this command. Two of its six tests assert the report-only invariant via `/report-only|drift report|does not delete worktrees/i` and **will pass falsely** after the extension if left alone, because the phrase "drift report" survives. They must be rewritten to assert the new contract, not merely updated to keep passing.

Tool names introduced into command prose (`adv_worktree_cleanup`, `adv_status`, `adv_worktree_delete`) are already registered, so `tool-name-assets.test.ts:70–104` passes. No new `skill("…")` literal is added, so the `SKILL_REF_INVENTORY` set-equality assertion is unaffected. No gate-handoff spine is added — `commands-spine-assets.test.ts` excludes this command from `expectedSpineFiles` and bans `## Next`/`## Next stage` headings.

### Out of scope

No changes to `adv_worktree_delete`, `adv_worktree_cleanup`, `adv_worktree_triage`, or `adv_status` tool behavior. This is a consumer-side orchestration extension only.

# Executive Summary

## Outcome

`/adv-cleanup` now shows you every kind of cleanup debt in one run and can act on all of it, instead of showing half and making you finish the job by hand. You are approving a change to an internal maintenance command that gains the ability to delete git worktrees and merged branches — behind a deliberately harder confirmation than the command's existing actions.

## Why It Matters

Before this change the command surfaced stale work items and mentioned drifted worktrees, but could not act on the worktrees and never looked at merged leftover branches or orphaned internal records at all. Anyone cleaning up had to run three more tools by hand, and would not have known the last two categories existed. This project currently carries 52 open work items, so the gap is not theoretical.

The change also closes a safety gap that predated it. The command's worktree categories (safe, blocked, dirty, needs-investigation) were labels the underlying tool never actually produces — it reports eight different technical states. That mismatch was harmless while the categories only fed a report. This change would have made those invented labels the gate deciding what gets deleted. Review caught it and added an explicit, source-derived mapping, so deletion eligibility is now decided by categories the tool genuinely emits, with anything unrecognized refused by default.

## Verdict

APPROVED

## What Was Built

1. One command run now covers four kinds of cleanup debt: stale work items, drifted worktrees, merged leftover branches, and orphaned internal records. Previously only the first was actionable and the second was mention-only.
2. Worktree and branch cleanup can now be carried out from inside the command, removing the need to hand-run separate tools.
3. Destructive actions are held to a higher bar than reversible ones. Reversible cleanup keeps its existing one-word approval. Deleting worktrees or branches requires typing a confirmation containing the exact number of items listed, so it cannot be approved from memory without reading the report — the same safeguard `terraform destroy` uses.
4. Every item proposed for deletion is listed by its full name or path, never as a bare count, and each is labelled with whether it can be undone and how.
5. Deletion is always carried out by the existing safety-checked tools, which independently re-verify before removing anything; their refusals are shown as-is rather than worked around.
6. The rules were written into durable project law (`rq-cleanupHygieneScope01`), which previously had no governing requirement at all.

## What Was Verified

- Verdict: APPROVED with 9 findings (2 blockers, 3 issues, 4 suggestions); all blockers and issues fixed and re-verified, 0 unresolved
- Harden added one further safety fix (see Release Readiness Summary), taking the guard suite to 69 tests
- Tests: `pnpm run check` clean including type, lint and formatting (run `tr_mse5qhju_c450dccb`, exit 0); command guard suite 69/69 (run `tr_mse5obxj_d1f4fb24`, exit 0)
- Full suite post-rebase: 8,351 of 8,366 pass. One failure, `src/mcp-server/health-field-scope.test.ts:99`, is inherited from trunk and not caused by this change — proven by reverting all changed files to trunk content and reproducing the identical failure
- The command's own guard tests grew from 6 to 69, and were proven to genuinely detect the old behaviour rather than passing by coincidence
- Preview URL: not_applicable — no user-facing visual surface. This change modifies agent-facing command instructions, project law, and tests; there is nothing to render in a browser. Recorded in the contract matrix under AC1/AC2.
- Contract matrix: 22 of 22 required rows pass or respected; 0 failed, violated, or unknown

## Remaining Concerns

- **Accepted deviation.** The new project law was written straight into the branch's law file rather than registered as a tracked law change (NO_DELTAS). The rule itself is correct, verified, and reaches the main branch on merge, but the change history for it is thinner than usual. Operator decision at release: accept as-is and record.
- **Accepted deviation, pre-existing.** Trunk CI is red from commit `da0344dd` (#365), which broke `health-field-scope.test.ts`. This change inherits that red; its own scope is green. Operator decision at release: ship and note.
- **Non-blocking, pre-existing.** Four code-style warnings in unrelated internal files, and one configuration drift notice, neither touched by this change.
- **Process note.** The first verification pass checked a hand-picked list of tests and missed a real regression this change introduced. Running the full suite caught it. The narrowed list was the mistake, not the tooling.

## Supporting Evidence

Tasks tk-4a8638067257, tk-56a80b1f58f7, tk-487b323fcadf, tk-484dece9d8dc, tk-4e7528cf60ba. Test runs tr_mse5obxj_d1f4fb24 (guard suite 69/69) and tr_mse5qhju_c450dccb (full check). Design validated by an independent researcher against clig.dev, clispec.dev, and the documented behaviour of docker, git, kubectl, npm, cargo, nix and terraform. Safety findings verified directly against tool source at `plugin/src/tools/worktree/triage.ts:54-62` and `index.ts:3175`. Contract review matrix holds per-item evidence.

## Release Readiness Summary

**Verdict: READY.**

**Safety fix found at harden.** The irreversible merged-branch bucket instructed an unscoped `adv_worktree_cleanup({ mode: "archived_branches" })` apply. On a subset approval — the operator types `delete 1,3` to remove two of five listed branches — that call would have deleted *every* currently eligible branch, silently bypassing the typed count-matched confirmation the bucket exists to enforce. This is the exact failure mode the change was designed to prevent, reintroduced one layer down in the apply step. Branch deletion is now issued once per approved candidate with an explicit `changeId`, and both command and skill state that an unscoped apply must never be issued. Guarded by two new tests. Committed as `77634516`.

**Deploy/ops.** Deploy from merged trunk, never from the worktree. After merge: `pnpm run build`, then `./scripts/deploy-local.sh --fix`, then restart OpenCode so the plugin host reloads. `.opencode/command/adv-cleanup.md` and `skills/adv-cleanup/SKILL.md` are mirrored to the local install, so agents in other repos keep the old contract until that deploy runs.

**Docs.** `manifest.ts`, command frontmatter, `README.md`, and `ADV_INSTRUCTIONS.md` now carry one identical description that discloses both the four surfaces and the typed-confirmation deletion capability. A new test keeps the four in sync, closing the drift class that had already gone unnoticed once on this branch.

**Safety of the shipped contract.** Destructive paths require the `--execute` flag *and* a typed count-matched confirmation that rejects the reversible bucket's `approve all` token. Deletion is always delegated to `adv_worktree_delete` / `adv_worktree_cleanup`; `adv_worktree_triage` output is advisory and never deletion authority; unrecognized orphan classes fail closed. Archived/closed state leaks stay report-only and route to `adv_archive_purge`, which owns its own operator approval.

**Rollback and blast radius.** Revert is clean: six scoped files, no schema, storage, or data migration. Nothing executes on its own — the command is operator-invoked with no background sweep, so a defect cannot fire unattended. If a deletion did misbehave, worktrees are restorable with `git worktree add` and branches via the reflog window.

**Accepted deviations carried into release.** (1) NO_DELTAS — spec law written directly into branch `spec.json` rather than as a typed delta; law verified correct, audit trail thinner than standard. (2) Inherited red CI from trunk `da0344dd`; this change's own scope is green and the failure is proven not attributable to it. A separate change should repair the `temporal_health` regression on trunk.
